title: Solid-State Chemistry and Materials
description: Ionic crystal structures, lattice energy, defects, band theory, semiconductors and superconductors.
overview: Most of the useful materials of the modern world are solids with a defined structure: the silicon of chips, the perovskites in capacitors and solar cells, the layered oxides in batteries, the ceramics in engines and the superconducting wires in MRI scanners. Their properties, from color to conductivity to hardness, follow from how ions or atoms are arranged and from the imperfections in the arrangement.

This chapter describes the common ionic structures and the radius ratio guideline, lattice energy and the Born–Haber cycle, point defects and ionic conduction, the band theory of metals, insulators and semiconductors, and superconductivity.
objectives: Describe rock salt, cesium chloride, zinc blende, fluorite, rutile, perovskite and spinel structures.
Use the radius ratio and the tolerance factor to predict coordination and stability.
Calculate lattice energy with a Born–Haber cycle and estimate it with the Born–Landé and Kapustinskii equations.
Describe Schottky and Frenkel defects, non-stoichiometry, color centers and solid electrolytes.
Use band theory to classify metals, semiconductors and insulators, and explain doping and p–n junctions.
Describe superconductivity, the Meissner effect and BCS theory.

sections.title: Ionic solid structures
body: Many ionic structures are close-packed arrays of the larger ions (usually the anions), with the smaller ions in the **holes** between them. A close-packed layer stacks as ABAB (hexagonal close packing, hcp) or ABCABC (cubic close packing, ccp, which is the face-centered cubic lattice). For N spheres there are N **octahedral holes** (surrounded by six spheres) and 2N **tetrahedral holes** (surrounded by four).
The structure that forms depends on the **radius ratio** r₊/r₋. The cation should touch all its neighbors without letting the anions touch each other:

head: Structure
Description
Coordination (M:X)
Examples
rows: ccp anions, cations in all octahedral holes
Simple cubic anions, cation in the cube center
ccp anions, cations in half the tetrahedral holes
ccp cations, anions in all tetrahedral holes
Distorted hcp anions, cations in half the octahedral holes
A cation (12-coordinate) at the cube center, B cation (6-coordinate) at the corners, X at the edge centers
ccp O²⁻, A in 1/8 of tetrahedral holes, B in 1/2 of octahedral
table.caption: Common ionic structures.

body: The perovskite ABX₃ is stable if the **tolerance factor** t = (r_A + r_X)/[√2 (r_B + r_X)] lies between about 0.8 and 1.0. At t near 1 the cubic structure is ideal, and a smaller t tilts the octahedra. **BaTiO₃** is a ferroelectric used in capacitors, because the Ti⁴⁺ is slightly off-center and gives a switchable polarization. The high-temperature superconductors and the new halide perovskite solar cells are perovskite derivatives. In the **spinel** AB₂O₄, a *normal* spinel has A²⁺ on tetrahedral and B³⁺ on octahedral sites (MgAl₂O₄), and an *inverse* spinel has the A²⁺ on octahedral sites and half of the B³⁺ tetrahedral (Fe₃O₄, magnetite, Fe³⁺[Fe²⁺Fe³⁺]O₄). The preference follows the ligand field stabilization energy: ions with a large octahedral preference (Ni²⁺, d⁸; Cr³⁺, d³) go to octahedral sites.

example.title: Radius ratio
example.problem: Predict the coordination number in ZnS (r(Zn²⁺) = 74 pm, r(S²⁻) = 184 pm) and in CsCl (r(Cs⁺) = 167 pm, r(Cl⁻) = 181 pm).
example.solution: ZnS: 74/184 = 0.40, in the 0.225–0.414 range: tetrahedral, CN 4 (zinc blende or wurtzite). CsCl: 167/181 = 0.92: CN 8 (cesium chloride structure).

check.q: How many tetrahedral holes are there per anion in a close-packed array?
What is the coordination number of Ca²⁺ in fluorite, CaF₂?
In the perovskite CaTiO₃, how many oxygens surround each Ti⁴⁺?

sections.title: Lattice energy and the Born–Haber cycle
body: The lattice energy of an ionic solid can be calculated or measured indirectly. The **Born–Haber cycle** applies Hess’s law: it writes the formation of the solid from its elements in two routes, one directly (the enthalpy of formation) and one stepwise through gaseous ions. For NaCl:

head: Step
ΔH (kJ mol⁻¹)
rows: ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g), half of the bond energy
Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s), lattice energy U
table.caption: Born–Haber cycle for NaCl. U is found by difference: −411 − (107 + 496 + 122 − 349) = −787 kJ mol⁻¹.

body: Theory gives U from electrostatics. The **Born–Landé equation** sums the Coulomb attraction of an ion pair with the lattice factor (the **Madelung constant** M, the geometric sum over the structure: 1.748 for rock salt, 1.763 for CsCl, 1.638 for zinc blende, 2.519 for fluorite) and a repulsion term with Born exponent n:

body.eq: U = −(N_A M z₊ z₋ e² / 4πε₀ r₀)(1 − 1/n)

body: For NaCl (r₀ = 282 pm, n = 8) it gives −755 kJ mol⁻¹, in good agreement with −787 from the cycle, and the difference is mainly the covalent contribution and dispersion forces. The **Kapustinskii equation** estimates U for any ionic compound without the structure, from the numbers of ions per formula unit (ν), the charges and the radii: U = K ν |z₊ z₋| / (r₊ + r₋) × (1 − d/(r₊ + r₋)), with K = 1.202 × 10⁻⁴ J m mol⁻¹ and d = 3.45 × 10⁻¹¹ m (use r in meters). This lets a chemist estimate ionic radii of complex ions (thermochemical radii).

The cycle explains why MgCl₂ exists but not MgCl or MgCl₃. Making Mg⁺ saves energy, but the lattice energy gain of forming Mg²⁺ (about −2500 kJ mol⁻¹) far exceeds the cost of the second ionization (1451 kJ mol⁻¹). For a Mg³⁺, the third ionization energy (7733 kJ mol⁻¹) is not recovered.

example.title: Born–Haber calculation
example.problem: Calculate the lattice energy of KCl from: ΔH_f(KCl) = −437; sublimation of K +89; IE(K) +419; ½D(Cl₂) +122; EA(Cl) −349 kJ mol⁻¹.
example.solution: U = ΔH_f − (sublimation + IE + ½D + EA) = −437 − (89 + 419 + 122 − 349) = −437 − 281 = −718 kJ mol⁻¹. The value is smaller in magnitude than NaCl’s, because K⁺ is larger than Na⁺.

check.q: A Born–Haber cycle is an application of…
Why does Mg form MgCl₂ and not MgCl?
check.a: The lattice energy of MgCl₂ more than offsets the second ionization energy
wrong: Cl cannot take a second electron

sections.title: Defects, non-stoichiometry and solid electrolytes
body: Real crystals are never perfect. At any temperature above 0 K, some of the lattice sites are empty or misplaced, because defects increase the entropy and so lower the free energy. The equilibrium fraction of defects is about e^{−ΔH/2kT}, where ΔH is the energy to create the defect pair.

list: A **Schottky defect** is a pair of vacancies, one cation and one anion, keeping the lattice neutral. It occurs in compounds of similar ion size and high coordination number: NaCl, KCl, MgO. The density is slightly lower than the ideal.

A **Frenkel defect** is an ion that leaves its site and occupies an interstitial position, leaving a vacancy. It occurs when the cation is small and the lattice is open: AgCl, AgBr, ZnS. The density does not change.

**Non-stoichiometric compounds** deviate from simple formulas, with variable composition, because the metal can take more than one oxidation state: wüstite is Fe₁₋ₓO with x about 0.05–0.15, and TiO₂₋ₓ and the tungsten bronzes are other examples.

A **color center** (**F-center**, from German Farbe) is an electron trapped in an anion vacancy. It absorbs visible light: NaCl heated in sodium vapor turns yellow, and KCl turns violet. Radiation also makes color centers, as in smoky quartz.

body: Defects allow ions to move. An ion hops into a neighboring vacancy, and the net result is **ionic conduction**. A **solid electrolyte** is a solid with high ionic conductivity and negligible electronic conductivity. Examples: **β-alumina** (NaAl₁₁O₁₇, conducts Na⁺ in layers, used in sodium–sulfur batteries); **yttria-stabilized zirconia** (ZrO₂ doped with Y₂O₃, where Y³⁺ replacing Zr⁴⁺ creates O²⁻ vacancies that conduct oxide ions at 700–1000 °C: the oxygen sensor in a car exhaust, and the solid oxide fuel cell); AgI (above 147 °C the Ag⁺ ions are disordered) and lithium garnets such as Li₇La₃Zr₂O₁₂, studied for all-solid-state lithium batteries.

check.q: Which defect does not change the density of the crystal?
How does doping ZrO₂ with Y₂O₃ make it an oxide-ion conductor?
check.a: Y³⁺ replacing Zr⁴⁺ creates oxide vacancies through which O²⁻ moves
wrong: It makes the lattice cubic only

sections.title: Band theory and semiconductors
body: In a molecule, N atomic orbitals make N molecular orbitals. In a solid with N ~ 10²³ atoms, the orbitals are spaced so closely that they form continuous **bands**. The filled band made from the valence orbitals is the **valence band** and the empty or partly filled band above it is the **conduction band**, and the separation is the **band gap** E_g. Electrons conduct only if they can move into empty levels with a small change in energy.

list: **Metals** have a partly filled band (Na, with a half-filled 3s band) or overlapping bands (Mg). Conductivity is high and falls with temperature, as lattice vibrations scatter the electrons.
**Insulators** have a filled valence band and a large gap, above about 4 eV: diamond 5.5 eV, SiO₂ about 9 eV.

**Semiconductors** have a small gap (below about 3 eV), so thermal energy promotes some electrons into the conduction band, leaving mobile holes in the valence band. Conductivity rises with temperature: Si 1.12 eV, Ge 0.67 eV, GaAs 1.43 eV, GaN 3.4 eV.

body: The conductivity of an **intrinsic** semiconductor is tiny, and it is controlled by adding small amounts of impurities, **doping**. Silicon (Group 14) doped with phosphorus (Group 15) has extra electrons in donor levels just below the conduction band: **n-type** (negative carriers). Doped with boron (Group 13), it has acceptor levels just above the valence band, which accept electrons and leave mobile holes: **p-type** (positive carriers). Doping at parts per million changes the conductivity by orders of magnitude.

Where p-type and n-type regions meet, electrons and holes recombine near the interface, leaving a depletion zone with a built-in electric field. Current flows easily in one direction only, forward bias: a **diode**. A **solar cell** is a p–n junction in which absorbed photons with energy above E_g create electron–hole pairs that the field separates, generating current (silicon cells convert about 20–25% of sunlight; the theoretical limit near 33% for a single junction of about 1.3 eV). In a **light-emitting diode (LED)** the reverse occurs: electrons and holes recombine at the junction and emit a photon of energy near E_g, so the color is set by the gap (GaAs infrared; GaP green; GaN blue, whose development earned the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics). Direct-gap materials (GaAs, GaN) emit efficiently, whereas indirect-gap silicon does not.

example.title: Gap and wavelength
example.problem: Calculate the longest wavelength that can excite an electron across the 1.12 eV gap of silicon.
example.solution: λ = hc/E_g = 1240 eV nm / 1.12 eV = 1107 nm, in the near infrared. Silicon absorbs all visible light but not photons of lower energy than the gap, which is why silicon is opaque to visible light, and transparent to infrared.

check.q: How does the conductivity of a semiconductor change with temperature?
check.a: It rises, as more electrons are promoted across the gap

sections.title: Superconductivity
body: A **superconductor** loses all electrical resistance below a critical temperature T_c. Onnes found it in mercury in 1911 (T_c = 4.2 K). A current set up in a superconducting ring flows for years without a power source. Superconductors also expel magnetic fields from their interior, the **Meissner effect**, which makes a magnet float above one, and which distinguishes a superconductor from a perfect conductor.

Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer explained conventional superconductors in 1957 (**BCS theory**, Nobel Prize 1972). An electron moving through the lattice attracts the positive ions and produces a local distortion, which attracts a second electron: two electrons of opposite momentum and spin form a bound **Cooper pair**. Pairs behave as bosons and condense into a single quantum state that moves without scattering. A gap opens at the Fermi level, and thermal energy must exceed it to break the pairs, which sets T_c.

head: Material
T_c (K)
Notes
rows: First high-T_c cuprate (Bednorz and Müller, 1986; Nobel Prize 1987)
Above the boiling point of nitrogen (77 K)
table.caption: Critical temperatures.

body: The cuprates (YBCO) are layered perovskites in which CuO₂ planes carry the current. They are ceramics, brittle and difficult to draw into wire, and their pairing mechanism is still not fully understood, so they are called unconventional. They are **Type II** superconductors: they tolerate magnetic fields through a mixed state, in which flux enters as vortices, so they can carry high currents in high fields. Applications include the magnets of MRI scanners (NbTi cooled by liquid helium), particle accelerators and fusion devices, magnetically levitated trains and sensitive magnetometers (SQUIDs).

check.q: In BCS theory, Cooper pairs are…
check.a: Pairs of electrons bound through lattice distortions
Expulsion of a magnetic field from a superconductor
wrong: Zero resistance in a magnetic field

quiz.q: In a ccp array of 8 anions, cations fill half of the tetrahedral holes. The cation:anion ratio is
quiz.why: 8 anions give 2 × 8 = 16 tetrahedral holes, and half of them is 8 cations. This is the zinc blende arrangement; filling all of them would give the 2:1 ratio of antifluorite.

quiz.q: Mg²⁺ has radius 72 pm and O²⁻ has radius 140 pm. The radius ratio and the predicted coordination number of Mg²⁺ are
quiz.why: 72/140 = 0.51 lies in the 0.414–0.732 range, which is octahedral (rock salt). The inverted ratio 1.94 results from dividing anion by cation.

quiz.q: In Li₂O, which has the antifluorite structure, the coordination numbers of Li⁺ and O²⁻ are
quiz.why: Antifluorite swaps the ions of fluorite (Ca 8, F 4). The cations fill all tetrahedral holes (CN 4) in a ccp array of anions, so each anion has 8 neighbors.

quiz.q: A perovskite ABX₃ has r_A = 134 pm, r_B = 60.5 pm and r_X = 140 pm. Its tolerance factor t = (r_A + r_X)/[√2(r_B + r_X)] is about
quiz.why: t = 274/(1.414 × 200.5) = 0.97, close to the ideal cubic value of 1. Omitting √2 gives 1.37, and swapping numerator and denominator gives 1.03.

quiz.q: NiFe₂O₄ is a spinel in which Ni²⁺ (d⁸) has a strong octahedral site preference. It is expected to be
quiz.a: An inverse spinel: Ni²⁺ on octahedral sites and Fe³⁺ split between tetrahedral and octahedral sites
wrong: A normal spinel, with Ni²⁺ on tetrahedral sites
A normal spinel, with Ni²⁺ on octahedral sites and all Fe³⁺ tetrahedral
Neither, because ligand field stabilization does not affect site choice
quiz.why: An ion with a large octahedral preference forces the A²⁺ onto octahedral sites, which pushes half of the B³⁺ onto tetrahedral sites: the inverse spinel, as in Fe₃O₄.

quiz.q: Calculate the lattice energy of LiF from ΔH_f = −617, sublimation of Li +159, IE(Li) +520, ½D(F₂) +79 and EA(F) −328 kJ mol⁻¹.
quiz.why: U = ΔH_f − (159 + 520 + 79 − 328) = −617 − 430 = −1047. Forgetting the ½D term gives −968, adding the electron affinity instead of subtracting it gives −1703, and a sign error gives −187.

quiz.q: Which compound has the most exothermic lattice energy?
quiz.why: Lattice energy rises with the product of the charges and falls with the interionic distance. MgO has 2+/2− ions that are small, so it beats the 1+/1− salts and CaCl₂.

quiz.q: Unlike the Born–Landé equation, the Kapustinskii equation does not require
quiz.a: The crystal structure of the compound
wrong: The charges on the cation and the anion
The radii of the ions involved
The number of ions in one formula unit of the compound
quiz.why: The Madelung constant in Born–Landé is specific to one structure type. Kapustinskii works from ν, charges and radii alone, so it can estimate U where the structure is unknown.

quiz.q: Which of these is most likely to contain Frenkel defects?
quiz.why: Frenkel defects need a small cation and an open lattice, as with Ag⁺. NaCl, KCl and MgO have similar-sized ions and high coordination numbers, so they form Schottky defects.

quiz.q: Wüstite has the composition Fe₀.₉₀O. What fraction of its iron is present as Fe³⁺?
wrong: 10%, the fraction of vacant iron sites
20%, the number of Fe³⁺ per formula unit
11%, the vacancies divided by the iron present
quiz.why: Charge balance for 0.90 Fe: 2(0.90 − y) + 3y = 2 gives y = 0.20 Fe³⁺, and 0.20/0.90 = 22%. The numbers 10% (the vacancy fraction) and 20% (Fe³⁺ per formula unit) are not shares of the iron actually present.

quiz.q: NaCl heated in sodium vapor turns yellow. The color is due to
quiz.a: Electrons trapped in anion vacancies that absorb visible light
wrong: Interstitial Na⁺ ions absorbing in the visible
Cl₂ molecules trapped in the lattice
Cation vacancies that hold electron holes
quiz.why: Excess Na takes up Na⁺ sites and leaves Cl⁻ vacancies, each holding an electron: an F-center. The trapped electron has visible absorption.

quiz.q: In yttria-stabilized zirconia, 4 Zr⁴⁺ ions are replaced by 4 Y³⁺. How many O²⁻ vacancies keep the crystal neutral?
quiz.why: Replacing four 4+ ions with 3+ ions removes 4 units of positive charge. Each missing O²⁻ removes 2 units of negative charge, so 2 vacancies balance it.

quiz.q: A GaAs light-emitting diode has E_g = 1.43 eV. Using hc = 1240 eV nm, it emits at about
quiz.why: λ = 1240/1.43 = 867 nm, in the near infrared, as expected for GaAs. Multiplying by E_g instead of dividing gives 1770 nm.

quiz.q: Why does the conductivity of copper fall as it is heated?
quiz.a: Lattice vibrations scatter the conduction electrons more
wrong: Fewer electrons are thermally promoted across the band gap
The band gap widens as the lattice expands on heating
The metal begins to oxidize in air and becomes insulating
quiz.why: A metal has a partly filled band, so the number of carriers does not rise with temperature, while greater vibration reduces mobility. In semiconductors the carrier number dominates.

quiz.q: Why are LEDs made from GaAs or GaN rather than silicon?
quiz.a: They have direct band gaps, so electron–hole recombination efficiently emits photons
wrong: Their band gaps are always smaller than silicon’s
They cannot be doped n-type or p-type
quiz.why: In an indirect-gap material like silicon, recombination mostly releases heat. Direct-gap semiconductors emit light, and E_g sets its color. Silicon does have a band gap (1.12 eV); it is simply indirect.

quiz.q: What distinguishes a true superconductor from a hypothetical perfect conductor?
quiz.a: It expels a magnetic field from its interior (the Meissner effect)
wrong: It has no resistance above a critical temperature
It carries current without any applied voltage
It has a band gap at the Fermi level in all cases
quiz.why: Zero resistance alone would only freeze in whatever field was present. Active expulsion of the field is what makes a magnet float above a superconductor.

quiz.q: Why is YBa₂Cu₃O₇ (T_c = 93 K) so much more practical than Nb–Ti (T_c = 9.5 K)?
quiz.a: It can be cooled with liquid nitrogen (77 K) instead of liquid helium
wrong: It is ductile, and is easily drawn into long wires for magnets
Its superconductivity is fully described by the BCS theory of Cooper pairs
It is a Type I superconductor that tolerates very strong magnetic fields
quiz.why: T_c above 77 K allows cheap nitrogen cooling. YBCO is actually a brittle ceramic, unconventional, and a Type II superconductor.

quiz.q: In BCS theory, T_c is ultimately set by
quiz.a: The thermal energy needed to break Cooper pairs across the gap at the Fermi level
wrong: The temperature at which the lattice melts
The energy to ionize the metal atoms
The temperature at which the Meissner effect is first measured
quiz.why: Cooper pairs condense into a state that moves without scattering. When thermal energy exceeds the gap, the pairs break and resistance returns.

summary: Ionic structures are close-packed arrays with ions in holes. The radius ratio predicts CN 4, 6 or 8 (zinc blende, rock salt, CsCl). Fluorite, rutile, perovskite and spinel are the other key types.
The Born–Haber cycle gives lattice energy by Hess’s law (NaCl: −787 kJ mol⁻¹). The Born–Landé and Kapustinskii equations estimate it.
Schottky and Frenkel defects are vacancies and interstitials. They allow ionic conduction, which is the basis of solid electrolytes such as YSZ and β-alumina.
Bands arise from orbital overlap. Metals have partly filled bands, and semiconductors have a small gap. Doping gives n- and p-type material, and p–n junctions give diodes, solar cells and LEDs.
Superconductors have zero resistance below T_c, with the Meissner effect. BCS theory involves Cooper pairs; cuprates such as YBCO reach 93 K.

problems.q: Calculate the radius ratios and predict the structures: LiF (r(Li⁺) = 76 pm, r(F⁻) = 133 pm) and CsF (r(Cs⁺) = 167 pm).
problems.solution: LiF: 76/133 = 0.57, in the octahedral range, so rock salt. CsF: 167/133 = 1.26. The rule would predict CN 8, but CsF actually has the rock salt structure, so radius ratios are only a guide.
problems.a: LiF is rock salt (ratio 0.57). CsF is also rock salt, although its ratio exceeds 1.

problems.q: Use a Born–Haber cycle to find the electron affinity of chlorine from: ΔH_f(NaCl) = −411, sublimation of Na +107, IE(Na) +496, ½D(Cl₂) +122, lattice energy −787 kJ mol⁻¹.
A silicon crystal is doped with arsenic. Is it n- or p-type? Describe the band picture.
problems.solution: Arsenic (Group 15) has five valence electrons, one more than silicon needs. The extra electron sits in a donor level just below the conduction band and is easily excited into it. The material is n-type.
problems.a: n-type, with donor levels near the conduction band.

problems.q: A light-emitting diode emits at 470 nm. Estimate the band gap in eV.
problems.solution: E = 1240 eV nm / 470 nm = 2.64 eV: a blue LED, as in GaN-based diodes (InGaN).
